text.p: Jose Maria Olazabal's feet hurt so much last year he could hardly walk, let alone play golf.
It was just as painful for him to sit at home watching the British Open on television.
"I watched it quite a bit, thinking to myself that I might never play golf again," the Spaniard said on Monday.
Olazabal's well-documented struggle with injury appears to be almost over as he prepares once again for the British Open that he played every year for 12 years until a year ago.
His best performance was third in 1992 at Muirfield.
"Somehow I feel more attached to the Open than to the other majors because the crowds have always been very good to me."
"It was tough, very hard at times, that I could only watch," he said.

The Spaniard has played 11 events since he began his comeback at the Dubai Desert Classic in February, winning the Turespana Masters in the Canary Islands in March in only his third event after an 18-month break.
He finished no worse than 22nd in his events since then -- until he missed the halfway cut at the Loch Lomond World Invitational last week.
He said bad driving caused that setback. "I missed a few drives on the first day but on the second I missed three tee shots that cost me four shots.

"The rest of the game was nothing extraordinary, but okay. I would love to have played well and put myself in contention last week because that would have been the best thing for me to have done for this week."

Olazabal's recovery has been masterminded by German doctor Hans-Wilhelm Muller-Wohlfahrt, who dismissed the previous diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and said the problem was caused by a spinal hernia.
In a nutshell, Olazabal said, some of the nerves were pinched and were not delivering the right information to his feet.
A course of special exercises, sometimes up to six hours a day, restored Olazabal to the point where he could return to action.
"It is still not 100 percent but it is nothing at the moment to stop me from practising normally or playing golf," he said.
He conceded that when he began to play again, he was more worried about his feet than his score, until a time when his improvement meant he worried more about his score than his feet.
The transition came, he said, just before he went to the U.S. Open in June.
"Then I started to feel that my feet were getting stronger and the pain was not as bad as it was before," he said.

He still exercises, morning and night. "We have to keep working on everything until it gets back to 100 percent. Once it is 100 per cent, the doctor says it should not come back. I will just need occasional check-ups.".

He said he has been better prepared at earlier Opens. "Obviously I would like to feel a little more comfortable over the next two days. But I will be happy teeing off. I know that I will give my best. If it comes my way I will be a happy man."
